body.text: Compulsory super requires many of us to do both at the same time — to save while we are borrowing. It’s a bit like driving a car with one foot on the brake and the other on the accelerator.

It’s possible. I’ve done it. Like many young drivers of my era, I found myself at first putting one foot on the brake and the other on the accelerator when I switched from driving a manual to an automatic. It wasn’t a particularly good way to drive. It produced a lot of friction.
When it comes to super and mortgages, putting one foot on the brake while putting the other on the accelerator can be frustrating.
Here’s a letter I received at ABC Radio National’s The Economy, Stupid from Mel, who could just about manage her finances if she didn’t have to save while borrowing.

Hi Peter, I love your podcast. At the great age of fifty I am glad to finally realise that rather than a dusty maths exercise, “economics” is actually the wonderful cradle holding all the best ideas about the society we wish for!

My seventeen-year-old son listens to your podcast too, and I love the discussions it sparks for us. I work in disability care and support my teenage kids and my eighty-two-year-old father in my (mortgaged) home. It’s often precarious financially, especially when health flare ups limit me.

My superannuation is $270,000. It would pay my mortgage and give me financial security if I could access it early. Can you see a future where the government relaxes the rules around early access to super, so that single parents in a “sandwich” situation like mine can support their families with the financial security of paying off their mortgage (without waiting for the bank to come knocking for missed payments)?
Thank you!

Why on earth shouldn’t Mel be able to use her super to extinguish her mortgage? She’ll be able to do it when she turns sixty (if she declares she has stopped working) or when she turns sixty-five (whether she is working or not). Why shouldn’t she be able to extinguish her mortgage now when she is fifty, at a time when her finances are at their most stretched?

Yes. Taken together, Australian retirees are less financially stressed than Australians of working age. The 2009 Harmer Pension Review found it (back when employers’ compulsory super contributions were 9 per cent), the 2020 Retirement Income Review found it (back when compulsory contributions were 10 per cent), and the Grattan Institute found it in 2019 using data from the 2015–16 ABS Household Expenditure Survey:
Why are retirees on average so much better off financially than Australians of working age? In this week’s edition of The Economy, Stupid, Cameron Murray points out:

They usually don’t have dependent children. They don’t have school fees. They don’t have family holidays. And the evidence that people are much more well-off includes the fact that, on average, people save during retirement.

The big exception, as the graph illustrates, is Australians who have to rent in retirement. The Retirement Incomes Review ended up being something of a rent assistance review, because it quickly found that for non-renters super contributions of 12 per cent of salary would be too much. It recommended increases in rent assistance.

For retirees taken together, it found, “Under the legislated increase in the Super Guarantee to 12 per cent, the projected replacement rate for future retirees with typical working lives exceeds the suggested 65–75 per cent benchmark rate across most income levels.”

It’s an argument for giving people the option of contributing only 9 per cent to super through their employers, as One Nation wants, getting the rest as salary at the times of life when they need it most, perhaps moving back to the default 12 per cent contribution later when their finances have improved.
It’s an idea with an impressive lineage. Coalition treasurer Josh Frydenberg toyed with taking it to the 2022 election and got the Treasury to run the numbers.
Before she got rolled, Coalition leader Sussan Ley is reported to have been preparing to announce it after the 2026 budget, having got the Parliamentary Budget Office to run the numbers.

The idea of allowing early access specifically to assist with mortgage payments also has an impressive lineage. The quote I opened with is from the start of a speech by the director of Labor’s National Housing Strategy, Dr Meredith Edwards, in 1992. That’s right, in 1992, before the Superannuation Guarantee became law.

There’s little that ought to be controversial about allowing access to super to assist with mortgages. The biggest threat to prosperity in retirement is having to rent. A pretty major government inquiry established that pretty early.

It might be that, in a strictly financial sense, it is advantageous to borrow and save at the time (even though money sticks to the hands of financial institutions in both directions). It could be. Whether it is financially advantageous or disadvantageous would depend on the tax rates, mortgage interest rates and superannuation returns net of fees at the time.

But for someone like Mel, that’s not the point. She needs to extinguish her mortgage now, rather than wait ten or so years until she has retired. It is now that her finances are stretched. It is now that she is at risk of becoming a renter.

The idea she can’t be trusted with access to her money is unsupported by evidence. And even if it was supported by evidence (in our podcast, Susan Thorp refers to studies of pigeons), the way we have chosen to respond to that evidence is weird.
Here’s Cameron Murray again:

Cameron: You can withdraw all your super at age sixty if you retire, and in fact, most withdrawals from the super system come as lump sum withdrawals, people just emptying out their super account after they have a sixtieth birthday party.
Peter: We don’t trust people on, on their behalf, we don’t trust them to have access to the tin when they’re fifty-nine and three-quarters?
Cameron: That’s right.
Peter: But when they have a birthday, we say, “Here’s the tin. Open it. You’ll do the right thing”?
Cameron: That’s right. “You’ve had no experience managing your own money because we did it for you, now here it all is.”

He is right. We behave as if people aren’t rational (on the basis of limited evidence) right up until super preservation age, then, the minute they get access to their super, we behave as if they are completely rational and don’t need to be protected from the folly of frittering away their money at all.

Just because an idea comes from One Nation doesn’t make it bad. These two latest ideas — access to super to pay down a mortgage, and the ability to select a super contribution of 9 per cent instead of the default 12 per cent — could be lifesavers for some.
Most of us are unlikely to use them, and that’s fine too.

The super industry doesn’t quite know how to respond. On one hand, the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia says giving people early access to their super would be inflationary (It also says most people would not take advantage of it).

On the other hand, the misleadingly named* Super Members’ Council, says retiree super spending injects $121 billion a year into the Australian economy, implying it would be deflationary if retirees had less to spend in retirement:

Retiree spending from their super flows into supermarkets and food producers, transport providers, trades and construction businesses, tourism and hospitality operators, insurers and financial service providers, and essential household services across Australia
Anyway, on cue, the industry has restarted an advertising campaign designed to persuade us things are just right as they are.

Who’s funding the campaign, and for what purpose? Each question is important. Regulated funds are now only able to spend money in ways that they can demonstrate they expect to be in the “best financial interests” of their members. As I wrote at the time when the law was about to come into force, “Vanity advertising, or advertising for a group of funds, or advertising aimed at influencing public opinion won’t cut it.”
The costs per member would need to actually shrink, along with the charges to members, or there would need to be a documented case prepared as to why they should have shrunk.
APRA anyone? •

* As it happens, the Super Members Council is not a council of super members. It represents a group of funds, rather than their members — the funds that were members of the Australian Institute of Superannuation Trustees and Industry Super Australia. A separate body represents members of super funds, often advocating for them against the funds. It is called Super Consumers Australia.
